title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 88
paragraphs: So Darius son of Hystaspes had been declared king, and throughout Asia all but the Arabians were his subjects, having been subdued first by Cyrus and then again by Cambyses. The Arabians, however, never submitted to the Persians as subjects, but had become guest-friends when they let Cambyses pass through to Egypt—for without the Arabians' consent, the Persians could not have invaded Egypt. Darius made the most noble marriages possible in the estimation of the Persians. He married two daughters of Cyrus: Atossa and Artystone. Atossa had previously been the wife of Cambyses her brother, and then of the Magian; Artystone was a virgin. Besides them he married the daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus, whose name was Parmys; and he also took to wife the daughter of Otanes, the man who had exposed the Magian. Everything became filled with his power. And first he had a carving in stone made and set up, showing a man on horseback, and he wrote on it an inscription to this effect: “Darius son of Hystaspes, by the excellence of his horse,”—naming it—“and of his groom Oibares, obtained the kingdom of the Persians.”
